# Education in Nigeria
Nigeria's education system follows a structured approach beginning with six years of primary education typically starting at age five, leading to a first school-leaving certificate. Subjects at this level include core areas such as Mathematics, English, religious studies, agricultural science, and indigenous languages, with private schools additionally offering Computer Science, French, and Fine Arts. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) program, established in 1999 and monitored by the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC), ensures nine years of free and compulsory schooling comprising six years of primary and three years of junior secondary education. Secondary education consists of a six-year cycle divided into Junior Secondary School (JSS) and Senior Secondary School (SSS), where students study core and elective subjects culminating in examinations such as the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE). Federal and state governments sponsor secondary schools, with federal institutions ("unity schools") often regarded as elite due to merit-based admissions, while private and religious schools offer alternative environments often characterized by smaller class sizes and better facilities.
Tertiary education encompasses federal, state, and private universities that offer various undergraduate and postgraduate programs. Entry requirements usually include credits from secondary school certificates and passing scores in the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) examination. The Nigerian government continues to expand higher education by approving new private universities. Vocational education is overseen by the National Board for Technical Education, offering certificates such as the National Technical Certificate and Advanced National Technical Certificate. Apprenticeships are encouraged as vital for skill acquisition and community values development. Despite these frameworks, challenges persist including teacher shortages, inadequately funded literacy programs, regional disparities especially in rural and northern areas, and gender-based enrollment gaps exacerbated by poverty, cultural factors, and insecurity. Efforts to enhance female education and overall literacy rates are underway through government initiatives and NGO programs, with ongoing work to improve both traditional and digital literacy nationwide.
